slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: “John put John’s hat on John’s head.” — the name *John* is repeated too many times.
It is better to say:  “John put his hat on his head.”
The word *his* is used in place of the noun *John’s*.
A word used in place of a noun is a *Pronoun* (*pro* = “in place of”).

slides.text: A Pronoun is a word used instead of a noun.
examples: he runs  ·  she sings  ·  they listen
I, you, he, she, it, we, they  (nominative)
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs  (possessive)

slides.heading: Adjective Elements
bullets: An Adjective Element is a word or group of words that modifies a noun.
Adjectives and articles are adjective elements:  small lakes, the boy.
So are possessives (John’s hat) and appositives (Nero the emperor).
Anything that describes, points out, or limits a noun is an adjective element.

slides.heading: The Possessive
bullets: A Possessive is a noun or pronoun used to modify a noun different in meaning from itself.
“John’s hat” — *John* and *hat* name different things.
It may be a noun (John’s hat) or a pronoun (his hat).
A possessive may itself be modified:  poor John’s hat,  John’s father’s hat.
Not only ownership — also kind (a boys’ school) or authorship (Ray’s Algebra).
A group with “of” can replace a possessive:  the nest of the bird = the bird’s nest;  the light of the sun = the sun’s light.

slides.heading: Apostrophe Rules for Possessives
bullets: Singular noun — add ’s:  John’s hat, the ox’s horn, Moses’s slate.
Plural ending in s — apostrophe only:  the ladies’ car, the boys’ coats.
Plural not ending in s — add ’s:  the men’s farms, the children’s shoes.
A few words take the apostrophe only:  for conscience’ sake, for goodness’ sake.
A pronoun’s possessive never takes an apostrophe:  its, hers, ours, yours, theirs (not it’s).

slides.heading: The Appositive
bullets: An Appositive modifies a noun or pronoun by denoting the same object.
It usually tells the rank, office, or business:  “Milton the poet,” “Mr. Jones the mason.”
It names the same object — a possessive modifies a different one.
Set off by commas — unless it is unmodified, or modified only by *the*.
“Stephenson, the celebrated engineer, …” — described, so commas;  “Mr. Whitcomb the lawyer” — only *the*, none.

slides.heading: Analyze — Adjective Elements
slides.intro: Every adjective element — adjective, article, possessive, or appositive — attaches to its noun in the diagram.

rows.note: The adjective *Sweet* slants under the subject *sounds*; the article *the* slants under the object *ear*.
The possessive *Frank’s* modifies the subject *father*; the article *a* modifies the predicate-noun *merchant*.
*poet* is an appositive — it renames *Milton*, so it sits beside it in parentheses; the article *the* modifies *poet*.

slides.heading: Personal Pronouns & the Three Persons
bullets: A Personal Pronoun represents a noun and shows, by its form, its person — first, second, or third.
First Person — the speaker:  I, we.
Second Person — the one spoken to:  you  (older: thou, ye).
Third Person — the person or thing spoken of:  he, she, it, they.
Add -self for the reflexive forms:  myself, himself, themselves.
“He hurt himself.” — a reflexive turns the action back on the subject.

slides.text: A Possessive Pronoun represents both the possessor and the thing possessed.
examples: This house is ours.  (ours = our house)
That book is mine.  (mine = my book)
mine, thine, his, hers, ours, yours, theirs, our own

slides.heading: Possessive Pronoun or Possessive Case?
bullets: “That book is his.” — *his* stands alone for “his book”: a Possessive Pronoun.
“That is his book.” — *his* comes before a noun: the possessive case, an adjective element.
Before a noun (possessive case):  my, thy, his, her, its, our, your, their.
Only *his* serves both:  “his hat”  ·  “the hat is his.”
*its* is possessive case only — “its tail,” with no stand-alone form.
Both are pronouns — the use differs, not the part of speech.

slides.heading: Analyze — Pronouns in the Sentence
slides.intro: The author's own models. A possessive or article hangs on a slant beneath the very noun it modifies.

rows.note: *He* is the subject, *book* the object; the possessive *his* slants beneath *book* — the noun it modifies.
The possessive *Their* slants beneath the subject *horses*; the reflexive *themselves* is the object.
*Ours* — a possessive pronoun — is the subject; the predicate-noun *task* carries two modifiers, *an* and *easy*, each on its own slant.

slides.heading: Incorrect Language — Cautions
bullets: Do not use him, me, or her as a subject or predicate:  “It is I,” not “It is me.”
Avoid false forms:  his’n, your’n, our’n, you’uns — these are not English.
Put you first and I last:  “you and he,” “he and I” — never “I and him.”

rows.label: Personal
rows.text: Represents a noun and shows its person. Each takes three cases.
rows.examples: I / my / me  ·  he / his / him  ·  they / their / them

rows.label: Possessive
rows.text: Stands alone for both the possessor and the thing possessed.
rows.examples: mine, thine, hers, ours, yours, theirs

rows.label: Possessive
rows.text: Before a noun — an adjective element.

slides.heading: Two Uses of “Possessive”
bullets: The word *possessive* names two things — a case and a kind.
*his hat* — the possessive *case*: a personal pronoun before a noun (an adjective element).
*the hat is his* — a possessive *pronoun*: it stands alone.
Test — before a noun → case;  standing alone → pronoun.
The forms usually differ:  my/mine,  her/hers,  their/theirs.
Only *his* serves both — the one form to watch.

items: How do you tell a possessive pronoun from the possessive case?
answers: A word used instead of a noun.
A word or group of words that modifies a noun.
A noun or pronoun that modifies a noun different in meaning from itself.
A word or group that modifies a noun by denoting the same object.
First (speaker), second (spoken to), and third (spoken of).
One that represents both the possessor and the thing possessed.
Mine, thine, his, hers, ours, yours, theirs.
The possessive pronoun stands alone; the possessive case comes before a noun.
